query.original_query: order of symptom presentation anchoring bias LLM medical diagnosis primacy effect

sub_queries.semantic_query: primacy effect anchoring bias in LLM medical diagnosis due to order of symptom presentation, attention head and circuit analysis of recency bias in clinical reasoning
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the role of token position and presentation order in shaping clinical reasoning within large language models, specifically analyzing how primacy and recency effects manifest in medical diagnosis tasks. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we identify distinct attention heads and MLP circuits in the residual stream that preferentially weight early or late symptom tokens. Our analysis reveals that early-presented symptoms exert disproportionate influence on final diagnostic outputs, consistent with an anchoring bias, while recency effects are mediated by late-layer attention heads attending to final context positions. We find that these positional biases are not uniform across model layers; early-layer circuits encode symptom order as a feature, while later layers integrate this positional signal with semantic content. Results show that corrupting early token representations via activation patching significantly alters diagnostic predictions, whereas intervening on middle tokens has minimal effect. This work provides a circuit-level decomposition of order effects in clinical LLM reasoning, highlighting how superficial positional features can override medical evidence.

sub_queries.semantic_query: anchoring bias primacy effect in clinical diagnosis order of symptom presentation cognitive bias medical decision making serial position effect on physician reasoning
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the influence of the serial position effect, specifically anchoring bias and primacy effects, on clinical diagnostic reasoning. In a within-subjects design, physicians reviewed sequentially presented symptom lists for ambiguous clinical cases. Symptom order was manipulated such that diagnostically critical information appeared either early or late in the sequence. We measured diagnostic accuracy, confidence ratings, and the final differential diagnosis list. Results indicate a significant primacy effect: symptoms presented earlier were disproportionately weighted in final diagnoses, even when later symptoms contradicted the initial hypothesis. This anchoring to early information persisted despite explicit instructions to consider all evidence equally. Findings support the hypothesis that order of symptom presentation modulates diagnostic reasoning through an anchoring bias, consistent with dual-process models of cognition. The effect was more pronounced under time pressure, suggesting reliance on heuristic processing. These results extend the serial position effect literature to naturalistic medical decision-making and highlight potential sources of diagnostic error in clinical practice.

papers.title: Integrating clinical reasoning into large language model-based diagnosis through etiology-aware attention steering
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex clinical scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: This study proposes an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework that integrates structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis by identifying and steering attention heads crucial for etiology reasoning, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and reasoning focus.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework integrates etiology-aware attention guidance with authoritative clinical guidelines, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy, attention stability, and reasoning interpretability, holding strong potential for real-world clinical deployment in complex diagnostic environments.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines on the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort.
External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort confirms the framework's effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy in real-world complex scenarios.
The Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm successfully pinpoints attention heads that exhibit strong alignment with etiological reasoning.
Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of each component (CRS annotation, Etiology-Aware Head Identification, Reasoning-Guided Loss) for overall performance.
The framework enhances the model's attention stability and reasoning interpretability across diverse diagnostic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to a broader range of diseases and clinical scenarios.
Integrating multimodal data (e.g., medical images, lab waveforms) to enhance diagnostic reasoning.
Incorporating contrastive or self-supervised objectives to further enhance model robustness in low-resource or noisy environments.
papers.abstract: Objective: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant capabilities in medical text understanding and generation. However, their diagnostic reliability in complex clinical scenarios remains limited. This study aims to enhance LLMs' diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability. Method: We propose an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework to integrate structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis. Specifically, we first construct Clinical Reasoning Scaffolding (CRS) based on authoritative clinical guidelines for three representative acute abdominal emergencies: acute appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, and acute cholecystitis. Next, we develop the Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm to pinpoint attention heads crucial for the model's etiology reasoning. To ensure reliable clinical reasoning alignment, we introduce the Reasoning-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning that embeds etiological reasoning cues into input representations and steers the selected Etiology-Aware Heads toward critical information through a Reasoning-Guided Loss function. Result: On the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort, our framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines. External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort further confirms its effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Further assessments via Reasoning Attention Frequency indicate that our models exhibit enhanced reliability when faced with real-world complex scenarios. Conclusion: This study presents a practical and effective approach to enhance clinical reasoning in LLM-based diagnosis. By aligning model attention with structured CRS, the proposed framework offers a promising paradigm for building more interpretable and reliable AI diagnostic systems in complex clinical settings.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: Quantifying Symptom Causality in Clinical Decision Making: An Exploration Using CausaLM
papers.research_question: What is the causal influence of key symptoms (specifically 'chest pain') on diagnostic predictions made by clinical NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents a method to assess the causal effect of symptoms on disease prediction models by leveraging the CausaLM framework to generate counterfactual text representations and using the TReATE metric to quantify the causal influence.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the potential of causal inference tools to provide a richer, more principled understanding of model behavior in clinical decision support, moving beyond correlation to capture causal effects.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of the symptom 'chest pain' significantly shifts the model's predicted probability distribution for diseases like Bronchitis and Anemia.
The TReATE metric provides a more robust causal interpretation of symptom influence compared to correlation-based metrics like CONEXP.
The adversarial training approach successfully creates text representations that are agnostic to the presence of the target symptom, enabling counterfactual analysis.
papers.limitation:
The causal interpretation hinges on the fidelity of the adversarial training process; imperfect 'forgetting' of the target concept may affect the strength of causal claims.
Disentangling the effect of one symptom may oversimplify the true medical decision-making process, as patients often present with multiple co-occurring symptoms.
future_direction: Exploring multiple treatment concepts simultaneously and controlling for sets of confounding variables.
Integrating structured medical knowledge to ground the analyses more firmly.
Testing the approach on diverse clinical corpora to validate robustness and generalizability.
papers.abstract: Current machine learning approaches to medical diagnosis often rely on correlational patterns between symptoms and diseases, risking misdiagnoses when symptoms are ambiguous or common across multiple conditions. In this work, we move beyond correlation to investigate the causal influence of key symptoms-specifically "chest pain" on diagnostic predictions. Leveraging the CausaLM framework, we generate counterfactual text representations in which target concepts are effectively "forgotten" enabling a principled estimation of the causal effect of that concept on a model's predicted disease distribution. By employing Textual Representation-based Average Treatment Effect (TReATE), we quantify how the presence or absence of a symptom shapes the model's diagnostic outcomes, and contrast these findings against correlation-based baselines such as CONEXP. Our results offer deeper insight into the decision-making behavior of clinical NLP models and have the potential to inform more trustworthy, interpretable, and causally-grounded decision support tools in medical practice.

papers.title: Embeddings to Diagnosis: Latent Fragility under Agentic Perturbations in Clinical LLMs
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how clinical LLMs exhibit latent fragility under small, clinically meaningful input perturbations, and proposes a geometry-aware evaluation framework to probe this robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LAPD, a geometry-aware evaluation framework, and LDFR, a metric that captures latent representational instability in clinical LLMs under structured perturbations, revealing a gap between surface robustness and semantic stability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework to uncover latent diagnostic instability in clinical LLMs, with LDFR providing a geometry-aware signal for auditing robustness, underscoring the need for evaluation beyond surface metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Latent fragility is exposed under perturbations like masking and negation, even when surface metrics remain high.
LDFR shows instability that traditional metrics miss, with masking causing the largest drop in accuracy and LDFR.
Patterns of fragility generalize from synthetic notes to real clinical notes from DiReCT.
Different models exhibit varying levels of fragility, with smaller models like Mistral-7B being more vulnerable.
Entity masking induces sharp latent shifts and diagnostic flips, highlighting over-reliance on surface cues.
papers.limitation:
Synthetic notes may not reflect real-world clinical variability.
Using a fixed BERT embedding space may misalign with model-specific representations.
No expert adjudication of whether diagnostic flips induced by perturbations are clinically warranted.
future_direction: Explore non-linear boundaries via manifold learning.
Expand perturbation analysis to include more types.
Align latent shifts with expert judgments for validation.
papers.abstract: LLMs for clinical decision support often fail under small but clinically meaningful input shifts such as masking a symptom or negating a finding, despite high performance on static benchmarks. These reasoning failures frequently go undetected by standard NLP metrics, which are insensitive to latent representation shifts that drive diagnosis instability. We propose a geometry-aware evaluation framework, LAPD (Latent Agentic Perturbation Diagnostics), which systematically probes the latent robustness of clinical LLMs under structured adversarial edits. Within this framework, we introduce Latent Diagnosis Flip Rate (LDFR), a model-agnostic diagnostic signal that captures representational instability when embeddings cross decision boundaries in PCA-reduced latent space. Clinical notes are generated using a structured prompting pipeline grounded in diagnostic reasoning, then perturbed along four axes: masking, negation, synonym replacement, and numeric variation to simulate common ambiguities and omissions. We compute LDFR across both foundation and clinical LLMs, finding that latent fragility emerges even under minimal surface-level changes. Finally, we validate our findings on 90 real clinical notes from the DiReCT benchmark (MIMIC-IV), confirming the generalizability of LDFR beyond synthetic settings. Our results reveal a persistent gap between surface robustness and semantic stability, underscoring the importance of geometry-aware auditing in safety-critical clinical AI.

papers.title: Eliminating Position Bias of Language Models: A Mechanistic Approach
papers.research_question: How can position bias in language models be eliminated without training, using a mechanistic approach?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PINE, a training-free method that eliminates position bias in language models by making inter-document attention bidirectional and re-assigning document positions based on attention-derived importance scores.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel train-free zero-shot approach to eliminate position bias mechanically by making every input document equally affected by attention mask and position embedding.
papers.key_findings:
Position bias in language models is caused by causal attention and position embedding.
PINE eliminates position bias and improves model performance on LM-as-a-judge, retrieval-augmented QA, molecule generation, and math reasoning tasks.
PINE is particularly effective for reasoning tasks, enabling Llama-3-70B-Instruct to outperform GPT-4 models on the RewardBench reasoning set.
PINE outperforms baseline methods such as PCW and Structured Prompting.
PINE incurs acceptable computational overhead (2x to 8x wall time) and memory cost.
papers.limitation: PINE requires extra computation overhead (2x to 8x wall time compared to vanilla inference).
future_direction: Improving the efficiency of PINE with more efficient implementation.
papers.abstract: Position bias has proven to be a prevalent issue of modern language models (LMs), where the models prioritize content based on its position within the given context. This bias often leads to unexpected model failures and hurts performance, robustness, and reliability across various applications. Our mechanistic analysis attributes the position bias to two components employed in nearly all state-of-the-art LMs: causal attention and relative positional encodings. Based on the analyses, we propose to eliminate position bias (e.g., different retrieved documents' orders in QA affect performance) with a training-free zero-shot approach. Our method changes the causal attention to bidirectional attention between documents and utilizes model attention values to decide the relative orders of documents instead of using the order provided in input prompts, therefore enabling Position-INvariant inferencE (PINE) at the document level. By eliminating position bias, models achieve better performance and reliability in downstream tasks, including LM-as-a-judge, retrieval-augmented QA, molecule generation, and math reasoning. Notably, PINE is especially useful when adapting LMs for evaluating reasoning pairs: it consistently provides 8 to 10 percentage points performance gains, making Llama-3-70B-Instruct perform even better than GPT-4-0125-preview and GPT-4o-2024-08-06 on the RewardBench reasoning set.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility: A Representational Analysis of Content Effects
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concepts of validity and plausibility, and why do they conflate them, leading to content effects in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that validity and plausibility are linearly represented and aligned in LLMs, causing content effects, and that steering vectors can disentangle these concepts to reduce bias and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The representational entanglement of validity and plausibility in LLMs leads to content effects, and representational interventions offer a way to mitigate these biases for more logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit content effects where plausibility influences validity judgments, especially in zero-shot settings.
Validity and plausibility are linearly encoded as single directions in the model's activation space, and these vectors are highly similar.
The degree of alignment between validity and plausibility vectors predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models.
Plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgments, and vice versa, demonstrating cross-concept influence.
Debiasing steering vectors that disentangle validity from plausibility can reduce content effects and improve reasoning accuracy.
papers.abstract: Both humans and large language models (LLMs) exhibit content effects: biases in which the plausibility of the semantic content of a reasoning problem influences judgments regarding its logical validity. While this phenomenon in humans is best explained by the dual-process theory of reasoning, the mechanisms behind content effects in LLMs remain unclear. In this work, we address this issue by investigating how LLMs encode the concepts of validity and plausibility within their internal representations. We show that both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity. Using steering vectors, we demonstrate that plausibility vectors can causally bias validity judgements, and vice versa, and that the degree of alignment between these two concepts predicts the magnitude of behavioral content effects across models. Finally, we construct debiasing vectors that disentangle these concepts, reducing content effects and improving reasoning accuracy. Our findings advance understanding of how abstract logical concepts are represented in LLMs and highlight representational interventions as a path toward more logical systems.

papers.title: Mapping Clinical Doubt: Locating Linguistic Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: How are epistemic signals encoding linguistic uncertainty represented across the layers of LLMs, and are these representations stable across model variants?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layer-wise probing metric, and demonstrates that LLMs encode linguistic uncertainty progressively in deeper layers, with sensitivity increasing monotonically with depth.
papers.conclusion: Encoding of epistemic uncertainty is a distributed and emergent property in transformer architectures, peaking in final layers, and the MSU metric provides a targeted lens for interpretability and epistemic awareness.
papers.key_findings:
MSU scores increase monotonically with depth across all tested models, indicating greater sensitivity to epistemic uncertainty in later layers.
PCA reveals clustering and geometric inversion in deeper layers, suggesting semantic reorganization of uncertainty representations.
Later layers exhibit substantially higher sensitivity to epistemic modals, aligning with their role in encoding abstract semantics.
The pattern of late-emerging sensitivity is consistent across different model families and instruction-tuning variants.
Uncertainty is treated as a high-level semantic feature that is progressively amplified across the transformer stack.
papers.limitation: Findings are based on a limited set of instruction-tuned models, so their generality across architectures, sizes, and pretraining paradigms remains uncertain.
future_direction: Expand to diverse model types, including non-instruct, multilingual, and domain-specific models.
Localize uncertainty to specific neurons or attention heads.
Examine how internal uncertainty signals (e.g., logits, entropy) relate to output confidence and calibration.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, where sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty can influence diagnostic interpretation and decision-making. Yet little is known about where such epistemic cues are internally represented within these models. Distinct from uncertainty quantification, which measures output confidence, this work examines input-side representational sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty in medical text. We curate a contrastive dataset of clinical statements varying in epistemic modality (e.g., 'is consistent with' vs. 'may be consistent with') and propose Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layerwise probing metric that quantifies activation-level shifts induced by uncertainty cues. Our results show that LLMs exhibit structured, depth-dependent sensitivity to clinical uncertainty, suggesting that epistemic information is progressively encoded in deeper layers. These findings reveal how linguistic uncertainty is internally represented in LLMs, offering insight into their interpretability and epistemic reliability.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: Dissecting Role Cognition in Medical LLMs via Neuronal Ablation
papers.research_question: Whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style.
papers.core_contribution: Role-playing prompts in LLMs do not induce role-specific reasoning pathways; they only affect surface-level linguistic style without altering the core decision-making mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Role-playing prompts primarily alter language style rather than enabling models to replicate the cognitive processes of real doctors, highlighting the limitations of current methods for building reliable cognitive agents in medical AI.
papers.key_findings:
Role-playing prompts do not significantly improve the medical reasoning accuracy of LLMs across multiple datasets and model scales.
Neuron ablation experiments show similar performance degradation across different roles, indicating a lack of role-specific cognitive pathways.
Representation analysis (CKA, PCA) reveals high similarity and overlapping clusters in hidden states across different roles, showing no hierarchical cognitive differentiation.
Jensen-Shannon Divergence analysis shows role effects are concentrated in early to middle layers and attenuate with depth, not affecting deeper reasoning structures.
Current Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP) methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity and differentiated reasoning strategies of real-world medical professionals.
future_direction: Developing models that go beyond language imitation and incorporate cognitive modeling techniques.
Integrating domain-specific knowledge into the training process and designing systems that can simulate the reasoning strategies of different medical professionals.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have gained significant traction in medical decision support systems, particularly in the context of medical question answering and role-playing simulations. A common practice, Prompt-Based Role Playing (PBRP), instructs models to adopt different clinical roles (e.g., medical students, residents, attending physicians) to simulate varied professional behaviors. However, the impact of such role prompts on model reasoning capabilities remains unclear. This study introduces the RP-Neuron-Activated Evaluation Framework(RPNA) to evaluate whether role prompts induce distinct, role-specific cognitive processes in LLMs or merely modify linguistic style. We test this framework on three medical QA datasets, employing neuron ablation and representation analysis techniques to assess changes in reasoning pathways. Our results demonstrate that role prompts do not significantly enhance the medical reasoning abilities of LLMs. Instead, they primarily affect surface-level linguistic features, with no evidence of distinct reasoning pathways or cognitive differentiation across clinical roles. Despite superficial stylistic changes, the core decision-making mechanisms of LLMs remain uniform across roles, indicating that current PBRP methods fail to replicate the cognitive complexity found in real-world medical practice. This highlights the limitations of role-playing in medical AI and emphasizes the need for models that simulate genuine cognitive processes rather than linguistic imitation.We have released the related code in the following repository:https: //github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/RolePlay_LLMDoctor

papers.title: Unveiling Confirmation Bias in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does confirmation bias affect chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs, and why does its influence vary across questions, reasoning types, and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that confirmation bias is pervasive in LLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning, affecting both reasoning generation and answer prediction, and explains variance in CoT effectiveness across tasks and models.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that confirmation bias significantly impacts CoT reasoning in LLMs, explaining performance variance across tasks and models, and highlights the difficulty of debiasing strong beliefs.
papers.key_findings:
Internal beliefs (approximated by direct QA probabilities) significantly influence CoT performance at both reasoning generation and answer prediction stages.
Questions with stronger beliefs (lower entropy) are more likely to retain correctness regardless of difficulty, showing confirmation bias.
CoT improvement aligns with the degree to which tasks are prone to confirmation bias, with greater improvement on symbolic reasoning (e.g., math) than on non-symbolic tasks.
Models with weaker beliefs (higher entropy) are more sensitive to the quality and structure of the generated rationale.
Debiasing internal beliefs is challenging, especially when beliefs are strong, as models struggle to follow rationales that contradict their confident prior beliefs.
papers.limitation: The use of entropy as a proxy for belief strength limits analysis to white-box LLMs and multiple-choice questions.
future_direction: Explore confirmation bias using confidence measures applicable to black-box LLMs and open-ended questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been widely adopted to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).However, the effectiveness of CoT reasoning is inconsistent across tasks with different reasoning types.This work presents a novel perspective to understand CoT behavior through the lens of confirmation bias in cognitive psychology.Specifically, we examine how model internal beliefs, approximated by direct questionanswering probabilities, affect both reasoning generation (Q R) and reasoning-guided answer prediction (QR A) in CoT.By decomposing CoT into a two-stage process, we conduct a thorough correlation analysis in model beliefs, rationale attributes, and stage-wise performance.Our results provide strong evidence of confirmation bias in LLMs, such that model beliefs not only skew the reasoning process but also influence how rationales are utilized for answer prediction.Furthermore, the interplay between task vulnerability to confirmation bias and the strength of beliefs also provides explanations for CoT effectiveness across reasoning tasks and models.Overall, this study provides a valuable insight for the needs of better prompting strategies that mitigate confirmation bias to enhance reasoning performance.Code is available at https://github.com/yuewan2/biasedcot.

papers.title: Elucidating Mechanisms of Demographic Bias in LLMs for Healthcare
papers.research_question: Can we identify activations within LLMs that encode sociodemographic information (e.g., gender, race)? Is the internal LLM encoding of patient demographics like gender and race localized, and can we intervene upon it?
papers.core_contribution: Gender information is highly localized in MLP layers and can be reliably manipulated via activation patching, while race information is more distributed but still intervenable. This allows studying and potentially mitigating implicit biases in clinical tasks.
papers.conclusion: Gender information is highly localized in LLMs, while race information is somewhat localized but more distributed. Implicit biases in clinical tasks can be studied by mechanistically controlling demographics, pointing to directions for future work and potential bias mitigation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Gender information is highly localized in MLP layers and can be reliably manipulated via activation patching.
Race representations are more distributed but can still be intervened upon to some degree.
Activation patching can alter generated clinical vignettes for specific conditions and influence downstream clinical predictions like depression risk.
The interventions do not significantly degrade text quality (perplexity remains similar).
Implicit biases in clinical tasks (depression risk, differential diagnosis) can be studied by mechanistically controlling demographics.
papers.limitation:
Did not extensively edit prompts, which can substantially affect results
Simplistic view of demographic categories, focusing on binary gender categories
future_direction: Extend to more inclusive demographic categories
papers.abstract: We know from prior work that LLMs encode social biases, and that this manifests in clinical tasks. In this work we adopt tools from mechanistic interpretability to unveil sociodemographic representations and biases within LLMs in the context of healthcare. Specifically, we ask: Can we identify activations within LLMs that encode sociodemographic information (e.g., gender, race)? We find that gender information is highly localized in MLP layers and can be reliably manipulated at inference time via patching. Such interventions can surgically alter generated clinical vignettes for specific conditions, and also influence downstream clinical predictions which correlate with gender, e.g., patient risk of depression. We find that representation of patient race is somewhat more distributed, but can also be intervened upon, to a degree. To our knowledge, this is the first application of mechanistic interpretability methods to LLMs for healthcare.

papers.title: CBEval: A framework for evaluating and interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive biases manifest in large language models, and can they be interpreted using a framework based on Shapley value analysis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a framework (CBE VAL) using Shapley value analysis to interpret and understand a host of cognitive biases in frontier LLMs, introducing round number bias and the concept of a cognitive bias barrier.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully interprets cognitive shortcomings in LLMs, revealing biases that arise from training heuristics, model characteristics like in-context learning, and the training data itself, similar to human cognitive biases.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit several cognitive biases including framing effect, anchoring effect, representativeness heuristic, priming effect, and a newly identified round number bias.
Shapley value analysis can be used to construct influence graphs that identify the words and phrases most responsible for the manifested biases.
A cognitive bias barrier is identified, representing the point at which an LLM understands a lower loss percentage corresponds to a higher profit percentage.
Models like GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini show differences in their cognitive bias barriers, indicating varying levels of robustness in decision-making.
Anchoring and priming effects, while similar, are hypothesized to rely on different model mechanisms: anchoring on the attention mechanism and priming on associative mappings in MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on output probability distributions; model responses can change due to token noise rather than actual reasoning.
Different system prompts produce slightly different probability distributions, though the main findings hold.
For some models (Mistral Large, Claude, Google Gemini), the API does not provide token probability scores, limiting analysis to subjective evaluation.
The experimentation was conducted prior to the release of the GPT-o1 model, so it is not included.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in Large Language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced their reasoning capabilities. Despite improved performance on benchmarks, LLMs exhibit notable gaps in their cognitive processes. Additionally, as reflections of human-generated data, these models have the potential to inherit cognitive biases, raising concerns about their reasoning and decision making capabilities. In this paper we present a framework to interpret, understand and provide insights into a host of cognitive biases in LLMs. Conducting our research on frontier language models we're able to elucidate reasoning limitations and biases, and provide reasoning behind these biases by constructing influence graphs that identify phrases and words most responsible for biases manifested in LLMs. We further investigate biases such as round number bias and cognitive bias barrier revealed when noting framing effect in language models.

papers.title: Medical Interpretability and Knowledge Maps of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent and process medical knowledge, and where is knowledge about patient demographics, symptoms, diseases, drugs, and dosages stored in the models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a systematic interpretability analysis of five LLMs for medical knowledge, integrating four techniques to build knowledge maps that show where medical knowledge is stored, and discovers phenomena such as non-linear age encoding, circular disease progression, and activation collapse in certain models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability methods can identify layers where medical knowledge is stored, and the findings can guide future fine-tuning, unlearning, or de-biasing of LLMs for medical tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Age is encoded in a non-linear manner with discontinuities (e.g., at age 18) in intermediate layers.
Disease progression representations are circular and non-monotonic, with late stages sometimes closer to early stages.
In Llama3.3-70B, drugs cluster better by medical specialty than by mechanism of action.
Gemma3-27B and MedGemma-27B exhibit activation collapse at intermediate layers, which recover by the final layers.
Most medical knowledge in Llama3.3-70B is processed in the first half of the model's layers.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground-truth data makes validation difficult.
For drug dosage, results are inconclusive and not well understood.
future_direction: Using knowledge maps to guide fine-tuning, unlearning, or de-biasing of LLMs for medical tasks.
Developing regularizers to enforce monotonic disease progression in models.
Further research into drug dosage representations.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic study of medical-domain interpretability in Large Language Models (LLMs). We study how the LLMs both represent and process medical knowledge through four different interpretability techniques: (1) UMAP projections of intermediate activations, (2) gradient-based saliency with respect to the model weights, (3) layer lesioning/removal and (4) activation patching. We present knowledge maps of five LLMs which show, at a coarse-resolution, where knowledge about patient's ages, medical symptoms, diseases and drugs is stored in the models. In particular for Llama3.3-70B, we find that most medical knowledge is processed in the first half of the model's layers. In addition, we find several interesting phenomena: (i) age is often encoded in a non-linear and sometimes discontinuous manner at intermediate layers in the models, (ii) the disease progression representation is non-monotonic and circular at certain layers of the model, (iii) in Llama3.3-70B, drugs cluster better by medical specialty rather than mechanism of action, especially for Llama3.3-70B and (iv) Gemma3-27B and MedGemma-27B have activations that collapse at intermediate layers but recover by the final layers. These results can guide future research on fine-tuning, un-learning or de-biasing LLMs for medical tasks by suggesting at which layers in the model these techniques should be applied.

papers.title: Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment of Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Earlier research has shown that metaphors influence human's decision making, which raises the question of whether metaphors also influence large language models (LLMs)' reasoning pathways, considering their training data contain a large number of metaphors. In this work, we investigate the problem in the scope of the emergent misalignment problem where LLMs can generalize patterns learned from misaligned content in one domain to another domain. We discover a strong causal relationship between metaphors in training data and the misalignment degree of LLMs' reasoning contents. With interventions using metaphors in pre-training, fine-tuning and re-alignment phases, models' cross-domain misalignment degrees change significantly. As we delve deeper into the causes behind this phenomenon, we observe that there is a connection between metaphors and the activation of global and local latent features of large reasoning models. By monitoring these latent features, we design a detector that predict misaligned content with high accuracy.

papers.title: Layer-wise Positional Bias in Short-Context Language Modeling
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether positional bias in language models is an intrinsic architectural property that persists across layers in short-context next-word prediction, independent of task complexity.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an attribution-based framework using layer conductance to analyze positional bias, showing that transformer layers exhibit stable, text-invariant positional importance profiles, with recency bias increasing with depth and early layers preferentially weighting content words.
papers.conclusion: LLM layers exhibit stable positional importance profiles in short-context next-word prediction, indicating positional bias is intrinsic to model architecture. Early layers assign the highest conductance to most words and prefer content words, while later layers lose word-type sensitivity and concentrate on recent positions.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer layers exhibit stable positional importance profiles in short-context next-word prediction.
These profiles are text-invariant and remain unchanged under lexical scrambling, indicating an intrinsic architectural property.
Recency bias increases monotonically with depth, while primacy bias is weak and diminishes in deeper layers.
Early layers preferentially weight content words over function words, while later layers lose this word-type differentiation.
Early layers dominate the largest proportion of words at all positions, while later layers increasingly concentrate importance on recent positions.
papers.limitation:
Focus on short contexts; may differ in long-context settings or tasks beyond next-word prediction.
Limited set of autoregressive transformer models; may not generalize to other architectures.
Reliance on layer conductance as a proxy for importance; different attribution methods may yield different results.
Word-type analyses based on POS categories and averaging; do not capture finer-grained syntactic or semantic distinctions.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to long-context regimes and tasks beyond next-word prediction.
papers.abstract: Language models often show a preference for using information from specific positions in the input regardless of semantic relevance. While positional bias has been studied in various contexts, from attention sinks to task performance degradation in long-context settings, prior work has not established how these biases evolve across individual layers and input positions, or how they vary independent of task complexity. We introduce an attribution-based framework to analyze positional effects in short-context language modeling. Using layer conductance with a sliding-window approach, we quantify how each layer distributes importance across input positions, yielding layer-wise positional importance profiles. We find that these profiles are architecture-specific, stable across inputs, and invariant to lexical scrambling. Characterizing these profiles, we find prominent recency bias that increases with depth and subtle primacy bias that diminishes through model depth. Beyond positional structure, we also show that early layers preferentially weight content words over function words across all positions, while later layers lose this word-type differentiation.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Estimating the Causal Effects of Natural Logic Features in Transformer-Based NLI Models
papers.research_question: How can we estimate the causal effects of semantic features (context monotonicity and word-pair relations) on transformer-based NLI model predictions, and what does this reveal about model robustness and sensitivity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a causal effect estimation framework for analyzing NLI models, measuring their sensitivity to relevant semantic feature changes and robustness to irrelevant ones. It shows that benchmark accuracy does not reflect these properties and that fine-tuning on a targeted dataset (HELP) can improve both robustness and sensitivity.
papers.conclusion: Causal effect estimation provides a granular view of model behavior, revealing biases and robustness issues not captured by benchmark accuracy, and demonstrates that targeted interventions can improve model reasoning properties.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar benchmark accuracy can exhibit very different behavior in terms of sensitivity and robustness to semantic features.
Models fine-tuned on the HELP dataset show improved robustness to irrelevant word-pair changes and sensitivity to relevant context changes.
Large models like roberta-large-mnli exhibit poor context sensitivity, indicating a bias towards upward-monotone contexts and ignoring negation markers.
Causal effect measures reveal that even high-performing models can systematically fail to adapt predictions to changing context structure, suggesting over-reliance on word relations.
Strategies to improve responsiveness to context changes (e.g., HELP fine-tuning) also increase robustness to irrelevant word-pair changes.
papers.abstract: Rigorous evaluation of the causal effects of semantic features on language model predictions can be hard to achieve for natural language reasoning problems. However, this is such a desirable form of analysis from both an interpretability and model evaluation perspective, that it is valuable to investigate specific patterns of reasoning with enough structure and regularity to identify and quantify systematic reasoning failures in widely-used models. In this vein, we pick a portion of the NLI task for which an explicit causal diagram can be systematically constructed: the case where across two sentences (the premise and hypothesis), two related words/terms occur in a shared context. In this work, we apply causal effect estimation strategies to measure the effect of context interventions (whose effect on the entailment label is mediated by the semantic monotonicity characteristic) and interventions on the inserted word-pair (whose effect on the entailment label is mediated by the relation between these words). Extending related work on causal analysis of NLP models in different settings, we perform an extensive interventional study on the NLI task to investigate robustness to irrelevant changes and sensitivity to impactful changes of Transformers. The results strongly bolster the fact that similar benchmark accuracy scores may be observed for models that exhibit very different behaviour. Moreover, our methodology reinforces previously suspected biases from a causal perspective, including biases in favour of upward-monotone contexts and ignoring the effects of negation markers.

papers.title: LayerNorm Induces Recency Bias in Transformer Decoders
papers.research_question: Why do Transformer decoders exhibit recency bias (attention bias toward recent tokens) when prior work shows causal self-attention alone induces a bias toward earlier tokens? How do other architectural components (LayerNorm, residual connections, input embeddings) affect this bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LayerNorm, when combined with causal self-attention, induces a recency bias in attention scores in Transformer decoders, and analyzes how residual connections and anisotropic input embeddings modulate this bias.
papers.conclusion: LayerNorm induces recency bias in Transformer decoders, providing insights for improving positional encoding strategies and length generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Stacked causal self-attention layers with LayerNorm induce recency bias, while without LayerNorm they do not.
Residual connections reduce the strength of the recency bias.
Anisotropic input embeddings (high cosine similarity between token embeddings) enhance the recency bias.
The recency bias depends on both query and key positions, not solely on their relative distance.
The theoretical framework extends to modern attention variants like MHA, MQA, and GQA.
papers.limitation:
Does not analyze the effects of feed-forward networks, other learnable parameters, or multi-head attention.
Does not evaluate the relationship between recency bias and overall model performance.
Does not examine the interaction with RoPE positional encoding, which is used in most modern Transformer decoder models.
future_direction: Exploring mitigation strategies, such as modifying the causal mask to counteract the uneven bias.
Design of future positional encoding methods based on these insights.
Research on length generalization in Transformer decoders.
papers.abstract: Causal self-attention provides positional information to Transformer decoders. Prior work has shown that stacks of causal self-attention layers alone induce a positional bias in attention scores toward earlier tokens. However, this differs from the bias toward later tokens typically observed in Transformer decoders, known as recency bias. We address this discrepancy by analyzing the interaction between causal self-attention and other architectural components. We show that stacked causal self-attention layers combined with LayerNorm induce recency bias. Furthermore, we examine the effects of residual connections and the distribution of input token embeddings on this bias. Our results provide new theoretical insights into how positional information interacts with architectural components and suggest directions for improving positional encoding strategies.

papers.title: Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon (U-shaped performance curve)? The paper investigates whether this behavior emerges from adaptations to short-term and long-term information retrieval demands during training.
papers.core_contribution: The lost-in-the-middle behavior in LLMs emerges from joint optimization on short-term and long-term information retrieval demands, and is influenced by architectural biases (autoregressive design) and attention sinks.
papers.conclusion: The lost-in-the-middle phenomenon is an emergent property from information retrieval demands, influenced by model architecture and attention dynamics, rather than a simple flaw.
papers.key_findings:
Training on free recall (long-term demand) yields primacy, on running span (short-term demand) yields recency, and joint training yields the U-shaped lost-in-the-middle curve.
Primacy effect arises from uniform long-term demand and is shaped by autoregressive architecture (causal masking), as shown by comparison with T5.
Recency effect directly aligns with the shape of short-term demand in training data.
Attention sinks support primacy under long-term memory demand; ablating them impairs free recall but not running span.
The effects generalize to masked sequence completion tasks, which more closely resemble next-token prediction.
future_direction: Uncovering connections between artificial and biological systems in memory phenomena.
papers.abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) often degrades when crucial information is in the middle of a long context, a "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon that mirrors the primacy and recency effects in human memory. We propose that this behavior is not simply a flaw indicative of information loss but an adaptation to different information retrieval demands during pre-training: some tasks require uniform recall across the entire input (a long-term memory demand), while others prioritize the most recent information (a short-term memory demand). Consistent with this view, we show that this U-shaped performance curve emerges when LLMs (GPT-2 and Llama variants) are trained from scratch on two simple human memory paradigms simulating long-term and short-term memory demands. Our analysis reveals that while the recency effect directly aligns with short-term memory demand in the training data, the primacy effect is induced by the uniform long-term memory demand and is additionally influenced by the model's autoregressive properties and the formation of attention sinks. Our main findings from simple human memory paradigms also generalize to a sequence completion task, which more closely resembles the next-token prediction process in LLM pre-training. Together, our findings reveal how information retrieval demands, model architecture, and structural attention dynamics during model training can jointly produce positional bias observed in LLMs.

papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
papers.research_question: Which reasoning steps (sentences) in a chain-of-thought are important for guiding the reasoning trajectory and final answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sentence-level analysis methods (black-box resampling and white-box attention analysis) to identify 'thought anchors'—critical reasoning steps that guide the trajectory of chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Sentence-level analysis provides a promising intermediate abstraction for understanding reasoning in LLMs, with methods converging to identify critical 'thought anchor' steps that structure the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have higher counterfactual importance than active computation or fact retrieval sentences.
Specialized 'receiver' attention heads consistently attend to thought anchor sentences, providing a mechanistic correlate of importance.
Sentence-sentence causal graphs reveal that stronger close-range links and weaker long-range links correlate with higher reasoning accuracy, especially in mathematical domains.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual importance metric can yield high-variance estimates when the number of semantically divergent resampled sentences is low.
future_direction: Investigating adaptive scales for defining reasoning steps beyond fixed sentences.
Further work on the limitations of the counterfactual importance metric with limited data.
papers.abstract: Current frontier large-language models rely on reasoning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Many existing interpretability are limited in this area, as standard methods have been designed to study single forward passes of a model rather than the multi-token computational steps that unfold during reasoning. We argue that analyzing reasoning traces at the sentence level is a promising approach to understanding reasoning processes. We introduce a black-box method that measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by repeatedly sampling replacement sentences from the model, filtering for semantically different ones, and continuing the chain of thought from that point onwards to quantify the sentence's impact on the distribution of final answers. We discover that certain sentences can have an outsized impact on the trajectory of the reasoning trace and final answer. We term these sentences \textit{thought anchors}. These are generally planning or uncertainty management sentences, and specialized attention heads consistently attend from subsequent sentences to thought anchors. We further show that examining sentence-sentence causal links within a reasoning trace gives insight into a model's behavior. Such information can be used to predict a problem's difficulty and the extent different question domains involve sequential or diffuse reasoning. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that our techniques together provide a practical toolkit for analyzing reasoning models by conducting a detailed case study of how the model solves a difficult math problem, finding that our techniques yield a consistent picture of the reasoning trace's structure. We provide an open-source tool (thought-anchors.com) for visualizing the outputs of our methods on further problems. The convergence across our methods shows the potential of sentence-level analysis for a deeper understanding of reasoning models.

papers.title: Anchored Answers: Unravelling Positional Bias in GPT-2's Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: Why do GPT-2 models exhibit a strong 'anchored bias' (consistently favoring the first choice 'A') in multiple-choice questions, and how can this bias be mitigated using mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper uses mechanistic interpretability (logit lens) to identify specific value vectors in MLP layers and attention heads responsible for 'anchored bias' in GPT-2 models during MCQ tasks, and introduces targeted interventions to update these vectors and recalibrate attention patterns, effectively mitigating the bias and improving model accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The work provides the first comprehensive mechanistic analysis of anchored bias in GPT-2 models, demonstrating that targeted, minimal interventions on specific internal components (MLP value vectors and attention patterns) can effectively mitigate this bias and enhance model robustness in MCQ tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 models (Small, Medium, Large, XL) exhibit a strong 'anchored bias', consistently favoring choice 'A' in MCQs regardless of correct answer position.
Specific MLP layers (e.g., layer 9 in Small, layer 20 in Medium) and attention heads (e.g., L8H1 in Small) are identified as key contributors to this bias via logit difference analysis.
Value vectors within the identified MLP layers, when unembedded, show a strong association with token 'A', indicating stored biased knowledge.
Directly updating the identified biased value vectors in the MLP's output matrix (W_out) using a simple formula significantly reduces anchored bias and improves MCQ accuracy across datasets.
Recalibrating attention patterns by swapping attention weights between the anchored position and correct answer position also mitigates the bias, especially for tasks like IOI.
papers.limitation: The paper notes that updating the identified value vectors to mitigate anchored bias may damage the model's performance on its original tasks (e.g., IOI, Greater-than), although the damage is shown to be acceptable in their evaluation.
future_direction: Exploring the impact of the proposed mitigation strategies on other tasks and model families beyond GPT-2.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), such as the GPT-4 and LLaMA families, have demonstrated considerable success across diverse tasks, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs). However, these models exhibit a positional bias, particularly an even worse anchored bias in the GPT-2 family, where they consistently favour the first choice 'A' in MCQs during inference. This anchored bias challenges the integrity of GPT-2's decision-making process, as it skews performance based on the position rather than the content of the choices in MCQs. In this study, we utilise the mechanistic interpretability approach to identify the internal modules within GPT-2 models responsible for this bias. We focus on the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers and attention heads, using the "logit lens" method to trace and modify the specific value vectors that contribute to the bias. By updating these vectors within MLP and recalibrating attention patterns to neutralise the preference for the first choice 'A', we effectively mitigate the anchored bias. Our interventions not only mitigate the bias but also improve the overall MCQ prediction accuracy for the GPT-2 family across various datasets. This work represents the first comprehensive mechanistic analysis of anchored bias from the failing cases in MCQs within the GPT-2 models, introducing targeted, minimal-intervention strategies that significantly enhance GPT2 model robustness and accuracy in MCQs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruizheliUOA/Anchored_Bias_GPT2.

papers.title: Stroke Lesions as a Rosetta Stone for Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can human lesion-symptom mapping provide external validation for LLM interpretability by comparing error profiles from perturbed LLMs to human aphasia data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the BLUM framework, which uses human lesion-symptom mapping as external ground truth for LLM interpretability, demonstrating that LLM error profiles under perturbation can be meaningfully mapped onto human lesion patterns.
papers.conclusion: BLUM provides a proof of concept for using human clinical data as external validation for LLM interpretability, opening a new methodological avenue for cross-system comparison.
papers.key_findings:
Symptom-to-lesion models trained on human aphasia data predict lesion location from error profiles with moderate-to-high accuracy.
Systematic perturbations to transformer layers in LLMs produce error profiles that fall within the distribution of human error profiles.
LLM error profiles map onto human lesion patterns above chance, with semantic-dominant errors predicting ventral-stream lesions and phonemic-dominant errors predicting dorsal-stream lesions.
Stronger correspondence is observed for sentence completion tasks compared to picture naming tasks.
Divergences exist, such as fewer phonemic errors in LLMs, indicating differences in computational strategies.
papers.limitation:
The present analyses are intentionally limited in scope to specific language tasks.
Divergences in error patterns between LLMs and humans, such as fewer phonemic errors in LLMs.
future_direction: Extend BLUM to richer linguistic features and more sophisticated architectures.
Direct investigation of whether behavioral alignment reflects shared computational principles.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities, yet methods to verify which model components are truly necessary for language function remain limited. Current interpretability approaches rely on internal metrics and lack external validation. Here we present the Brain-LLM Unified Model (BLUM), a framework that leverages lesion-symptom mapping, the gold standard for establishing causal brain-behavior relationships for over a century, as an external reference structure for evaluating LLM perturbation effects. Using data from individuals with chronic post-stroke aphasia (N = 410), we trained symptom-to-lesion models that predict brain damage location from behavioral error profiles, applied systematic perturbations to transformer layers, administered identical clinical assessments to perturbed LLMs and human patients, and projected LLM error profiles into human lesion space. LLM error profiles were sufficiently similar to human error profiles that predicted lesions corresponded to actual lesions in error-matched humans above chance in 67% of picture naming conditions (p < 10^{-23}) and 68.3% of sentence completion conditions (p < 10^{-61}), with semantic-dominant errors mapping onto ventral-stream lesion patterns and phonemic-dominant errors onto dorsal-stream patterns. These findings open a new methodological avenue for LLM interpretability in which clinical neuroscience provides external validation, establishing human lesion-symptom mapping as a reference framework for evaluating artificial language systems and motivating direct investigation of whether behavioral alignment reflects shared computational principles.

papers.title: Lost in the Prompt Order: Revealing the Limitations of Causal Attention in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism behind the performance gap between CQO (context-question-option) and QOC (question-option-context) prompt orderings in multiple-choice question answering for decoder-only large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The performance gap between CQO and QOC orderings in multiple-choice question answering is primarily due to causal attention masking in decoder-only LLMs, which prevents option tokens from attending to context tokens in the QOC order.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies causal attention as the key mechanism behind prompt order sensitivity in decoder-only LLMs for MCQA, providing mechanistic insight and practical guidance for prompt design.
papers.key_findings:
CQO ordering outperforms QOC by over 14% across 21 decoder-only LLMs and four datasets.
The gap is not explained by training data bias or failure to recall options.
Causal attention masking is the core mechanism: in QOC, the causal mask prevents option tokens from attending to context tokens, making context effectively inaccessible.
Encoder models with bidirectional attention show no performance gap, confirming the role of causal masking.
Targeted interventions (attention pruning, activation patching, option repetition) degrade CQO or improve QOC performance, further supporting the causal attention explanation.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are primarily focused on MCQA tasks with four-option formats.
Models are evaluated only up to 9B parameters due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit surprising sensitivity to the structure of the prompt, but the mechanisms underlying this sensitivity remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct an in-depth investigation on a striking case: in multiple-choice question answering, placing context before the questions and options (CQO) outperforms the reverse order (QOC) by over 14%p, consistently over a wide range of models and datasets. Through systematic architectural analysis, we identify causal attention as the core mechanism: in QOC prompts, the causal mask prevents option tokens from attending to context, creating an information bottleneck where context becomes invisible to options.

papers.title: Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment
papers.research_question: What causes negative bias in large language models during binary decision tasks requiring complex reasoning, and how can it be corrected through attention head analysis and tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Negative Attention Score (NAS) to quantify negative bias in LLMs and proposes NASA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that corrects bias by aligning attention heads identified via NAS.
papers.conclusion: NASA effectively mitigates negative bias in LLMs for binary decision tasks and serves as a useful interpretability framework for analyzing attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit negative bias in binary decision tasks, showing high precision but low recall and higher confidence for negative responses.
NAS correlates with negative confidence and identifies query-agnostic negative attention heads across domains.
NASA reduces the precision-recall gap and improves F1 scores while preserving general reasoning abilities.
NASA enhances model calibration by aligning prediction confidence with accuracy.
Fine-tuning negative attention heads in order based on NAS is effective, whereas random tuning leads to suboptimal results.
papers.limitation:
Further research is needed to understand the causes and mechanisms behind negative biases in LLMs.
Fine-tuning attention heads individually may not be time-efficient; more efficient training methods could be explored.
future_direction: Explore more time-efficient training methods for tuning attention heads.
Investigate integrated research approaches connecting various elements of negative bias.
papers.abstract: A binary decision task, like yes-no questions or answer verification, reflects a significant real-world scenario such as where users look for confirmation about the correctness of their decisions on specific issues. In this work, we observe that language models exhibit a negative bias in the binary decisions of complex reasoning tasks. Based on our observations and the rationale about attention-based model dynamics, we propose a negative attention score (NAS) to systematically and quantitatively formulate negative bias. Based on NAS, we identify attention heads that attend to negative tokens provided in the instructions as answer candidate of binary decisions, regardless of the question in the prompt, and validate their association with the negative bias. Additionally, we propose the negative attention score alignment (NASA) method, which is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique to address the extracted negatively biased attention heads.
